Layer 4 below 22.8 m has a resistivity of about 8,000 ohm-m and is interpreted as fresh basement. No clearly water bearing low resistivity zone is resolved at this point within the investigated depth. The depth to bedrock is estimated at about 0.8 m. The Dar-Zarrouk longitudinal conductance of the section is 0.0164 siemens and the transverse resistance is 40,200 ohm m2. This gives a poor protective capacity against surface contamination.
basement over compact rock.rationale: No water-bearing zone was resolved within the investigated depth, so the drilling prospect here is weak.

half-metre zone.narrative: The data at half-metre zone resolves a 3 layer subsurface (type H; a conductive layer between two more resistive layers, the classical signature of a saturated weathered zone above fresh basement). Layer 1 from 0 m to 3.5 m (3.5 m thick) has a resistivity of about 500 ohm-m and is interpreted as topsoil / laterite. Layer 2 from 3.5 m to 4.5 m (1 m thick) has a resistivity of about 100 ohm-m and is interpreted as weathered / fractured zone, potentially water bearing when saturated. Layer 3 below 4.5 m has a resistivity of about 5,000 ohm-m and is interpreted as fresh basement. The unusually low resistivity within the interpreted fractured or weathered intervals is indicative of pore electrolyte, possibly groundwater. The possible water zones are 4 m to 5 m. The depth to bedrock is estimated at about 4.5 m. The Dar-Zarrouk longitudinal conductance of the section is 0.017 siemens and the transverse resistance is 1,850 ohm m2. The cover overlying the water bearing zone has a longitudinal conductance of 0.007 siemens, indicating a poor protective capacity against surface contamination.
half-metre zone.rationale: Driven by about 1 m of interpreted water-bearing thickness (thin); resistivities near the edge of the productive window; a fractured zone at the basement contact; overburden of about 4 m that limits the target.

short sounding.narrative: The data at short sounding resolves a 3 layer subsurface (type H; a conductive layer between two more resistive layers, the classical signature of a saturated weathered zone above fresh basement). Layer 2 from 0.6 m to 8.6 m (8 m thick) has a resistivity of about 90 ohm-m and is interpreted as weathered / fractured zone, potentially water bearing when saturated. Layer 3 below 8.6 m has a resistivity of about 3,000 ohm-m and is interpreted as fresh basement. No clearly water bearing low resistivity zone is resolved at this point within the investigated depth. The water-bearing layer from 0.6 m starts within the top 3 m, which are taken as unsaturated, and the sounding resolves only 2.5 m, so it is not counted as a water zone. The depth to bedrock is not resolved within the depth of investigation (about 2.5 m). The Dar-Zarrouk longitudinal conductance of the section is 0.0904 siemens and the transverse resistance is 960 ohm m2. This gives a poor protective capacity against surface contamination.

doi_text: A Schlumberger sounding resolves the ground to roughly half its largest AB/2, not to the spacing itself: with AB/2 expanded to 80 m the depth of investigation here is about 40 m, and any structure below it is not resolved.

A Wenner sounding resolves the ground to roughly half its largest electrode spacing a, not to the spacing itself: with a expanded to 60 m (AB/2 of 90 m) the depth of investigation here is about 30 m, and any structure below it is not resolved.

A Wenner sounding resolves the ground to roughly 0.4 times its largest electrode spacing a, not to the spacing itself: with a expanded to 60 m (AB/2 of 90 m) the depth of investigation here is about 24 m, and any structure below it is not resolved.
sheets: The sheet is a Wenner sounding tabulated as AB/2. The Wenner array has AB = 3a, so each spacing was read as a = two thirds of the tabulated AB/2, which is the spacing the Wenner geometric factor and forward model take.

The sounding was read as Wenner, as the sheet has it, but its MN column holds spacings other than a and it repeats 1 spacing. A Wenner array keeps MN equal to the spacing a and reads each spacing once, so these are the marks of a Schlumberger sounding. Confirm the array with the field crew: the wrong forward model is wrong by tens of percent.
1 AB/2 value(s) read more than once; the readings are kept, and the inversion fits each one as it stands rather than merging them.
1 AB/2 value(s) repeated with different MN (segment changes); both readings kept.

At an MN change the two readings at one AB/2 should agree within a few percent; these differ by more than 20 percent: AB/2 40 m: 150 and 78 ohm-m (ratio 1.92). That is a field problem (potential-electrode contact, lateral inhomogeneity at the new MN) or a transcription slip, and the inversion merges the pair by geometric mean, so part of the model misfit is made by the splice. Check the sheet before relying on the deep branch.

Sheet 'S3 copy' carries the sounding number 'S 3', which sheet 'S3' already uses. A sheet copied without renumbering reads as the same point in every table, figure and ranking; give each sounding its own number before the results are used.
The sheet records a resistance (V/I), not a resistivity; apparent resistivity was computed as K x R from the electrode spacings.

The Schlumberger geometric factor K needs MN/2 between 0 and AB/2, so the resistances read at AB/2 0.3 and 0.5 m could not be turned into resistivities and are left out. Check the spacings on the sheet.
1 AB/2 value(s) read more than once; the readings are kept, and the inversion fits each one as it stands rather than merging them.

Readings repeated at one AB/2 should agree within a few percent; these differ by more than 20 percent: AB/2 10 m: 90 and 120 ohm-m (ratio 1.33). That is a field problem (electrode contact, an electrode moved between the readings, lateral inhomogeneity at a new MN) or a transcription slip, and the inversion fits each reading as it stands, so the disagreement is part of the model misfit. Check the sheet before relying on the model.

The prior is 43 percent (between 23 and 63), for the BGS class B-L on the USGS unit pCm: BGS Low productivity, 0.1 to 0.5 L/s (O Dochartaigh 2021, Table 3), which the guide describes, for the Africa-wide productivity map these maps develop, as roughly the interquartile range of the yields of boreholes sited and drilled using appropriate techniques (Table 4). No cited source separates the Precambrian unit within the class, so the class's yields apply. Read as the quartiles of a lognormal spread, 0.1 and 0.5 L/s put 43 percent of boreholes at or above 0.28 L/s. It is held as firmly as 10 boreholes would hold it, and has not been calibrated against boreholes drilled here.

text: A second sounding beside productive is worth up to US$ 26 to this decision and costs about US$ 100. It costs more than it is worth to this decision.

Without it, drilling at productive first is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 51 percent, against 30 at point productive. Drilling at productive, and going to point productive if it is dry, is expected to cost US$ 14,121 for a working borehole; going to point productive straight away, US$ 16,689.

The choice changes, to going to point productive, on the readings whose factors multiply to less than 0.40, which the measurement reads with a chance of about 4 percent. Taking the cheaper choice on each reading, the expected cost falls from US$ 14,121 to US$ 14,095.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at productive would work would be worth US$ 1,712 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.

The range of models has not been sampled at productive, so a second sounding is read, as this one was, for its water-zone resistivity alone, and is worth what a profiling line is; sample the range to count its depth to basement too.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (1). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

Without it, drilling at productive first is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 68 percent, against 50 at an unsurveyed site on the same ground. text: A second sounding beside clay is worth up to US$ 90 to this decision and costs about US$ 100. It costs more than it is worth to this decision.

Without it, drilling at clay first is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 48 percent, against 35 at point clay. Drilling at clay, and going to point clay if it is dry, is expected to cost US$ 13,601 for a working borehole; going to point clay straight away, US$ 14,951.

The choice changes, to going to point clay, on the readings whose factors multiply to less than 0.57, which the measurement reads with a chance of about 13 percent. Taking the cheaper choice on each reading, the expected cost falls from US$ 13,601 to US$ 13,511.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at clay would work would be worth US$ 1,826 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (0.8). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

text: A second sounding beside clayey is worth up to US$ 150 to this decision and costs about US$ 100. It is worth more than it costs.

Without it, drilling at clayey first is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 47 percent, against 43 at an unsurveyed site on the same ground. Drilling at clayey, and going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground if it is dry, is expected to cost US$ 12,642 for a working borehole; going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground straight away, US$ 13,007.

The choice changes, to going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground, on the readings whose factors multiply to less than 0.84, which the measurement reads with a chance of about 31 percent. Taking the cheaper choice on each reading, the expected cost falls from US$ 12,642 to US$ 12,491.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at clayey would work would be worth US$ 1,849 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (0.6). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

text: A second sounding beside resistive cannot change this decision: nothing it could read moves the chance at resistive past the alternative's, so it is worth nothing to it. It costs about US$ 100.

Without it, drilling at resistive first is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 97 percent, against 51 at point resistive. Drilling at resistive, and going to point resistive if it is dry, is expected to cost US$ 8,537 for a working borehole; going to point resistive straight away, US$ 11,638.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at resistive would work would be worth US$ 112 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (0.3). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

Without it, going to point fresh is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 36 percent, against 23 at fresh. Going there straight away is expected to cost US$ 14,569 for a working borehole; drilling at fresh first, and going to point fresh if it is dry, US$ 15,828.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at fresh would work would be worth US$ 1,439 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (1). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

text: About 23 percent (between 11 and 40) that a borehole here yields enough for a handpump through the dry season. Provisional prior.
Success means a yield of at least 1 m3/h (0.28 L/s) at the dry-season water level, the handpump design rate in the configuration.

The prior is 43 percent (between 23 and 63), for the BGS class B-L on the USGS unit pCm: BGS Low productivity, 0.1 to 0.5 L/s (O Dochartaigh 2021, Table 3), which the guide describes, for the Africa-wide productivity map these maps develop, as roughly the interquartile range of the yields of boreholes sited and drilled using appropriate techniques (Table 4). No cited source separates the Precambrian unit within the class, so the class's yields apply. Read as the quartiles of a lognormal spread, 0.1 and 0.5 L/s put 43 percent of boreholes at or above 0.28 L/s. It is held as firmly as 10 boreholes would hold it, and has not been calibrated against boreholes drilled here.

values.summary: A second sounding beside dry is worth up to US$ 594 to this decision and costs about US$ 100. It is worth more than it costs.
text: A second sounding beside dry is worth up to US$ 594 to this decision and costs about US$ 100. It is worth more than it costs.

Without it, drilling at dry first is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 25 percent, against 25 at point dry. Drilling at dry, and going to point dry if it is dry, is expected to cost US$ 18,735 for a working borehole; going to point dry straight away, US$ 18,735.

The choice changes, to going to point dry, on the readings whose factors multiply to less than 1.00, which the measurement reads with a chance of about 46 percent. Taking the cheaper choice on each reading, the expected cost falls from US$ 18,735 to US$ 18,141.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at dry would work would be worth US$ 2,622 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (1). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

text: A second sounding beside rounded is worth up to US$ 8 to this decision and costs about US$ 100. It costs more than it is worth to this decision.

Without it, going to point rounded is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 46 percent, against 30 at rounded. Going there straight away is expected to cost US$ 12,504 for a working borehole; drilling at rounded first, and going to point rounded if it is dry, US$ 13,740.

The choice changes, to drilling at rounded, on the readings whose factors multiply to more than 2.00, which the measurement reads with a chance of about 9 percent. Taking the cheaper choice on each reading, the expected cost falls from US$ 12,504 to US$ 12,496.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at rounded would work would be worth US$ 1,235 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (1). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (1). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

text: A second sounding beside rounded is worth up to US$ 68 to this decision and costs about US$ 100. It costs more than it is worth to this decision.

Without it, drilling at rounded first is the cheaper choice: the chance of a working borehole there is about 68 percent, against 50 at an unsurveyed site on the same ground. Drilling at rounded, and going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground if it is dry, is expected to cost US$ 10,581 for a working borehole; going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground straight away, US$ 11,825.

The choice changes, to going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground, on the readings whose factors multiply to less than 0.48, which the measurement reads with a chance of about 9 percent. Taking the cheaper choice on each reading, the expected cost falls from US$ 10,581 to US$ 10,513.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at rounded would work would be worth US$ 1,131 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.

Drilling at edge_fit_5, and going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground if it is dry, is expected to cost US$ 12,459 for a working borehole; going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground straight away, US$ 13,007.

The choice changes, to going to an unsurveyed site on the same ground, on the readings whose factors multiply to less than 0.76, which the measurement reads with a chance of about 18 percent. Taking the cheaper choice on each reading, the expected cost falls from US$ 12,459 to US$ 12,356.
Knowing for certain whether a borehole at edge_fit_5 would work would be worth US$ 1,771 to this decision; no measurement can be worth more.
values.basis: Basis: a working borehole is needed, so the choice is where to drill, not whether. The alternative is the other surveyed point with the best odds, or on a survey of one point an unsurveyed site on the same ground at the prior. Going to it is taken to cost its expected cost per working borehole, from the cost distribution's mean completed borehole (US$ 8,320) and mean dry attempt (US$ 3,505); drilling at the point first costs the completed borehole if it works, and the dry attempt and then the alternative if it does not. Both places are taken to cost the same to drill. What a measurement could read are the bands of success_evidence.yaml, its likelihood ratios raised to the weight of the point's fit (0.8). The ratios do not say how often each band is seen, so the bands are spread among dry boreholes as evenly as the ratios allow, and among working ones by the ratios; other spreads the ratios allow give other values, larger or smaller, so the even spread is a choice and not a bound. The readings are taken as independent of each other and of the readings already made, given whether a borehole at the point would work; a sounding beside the first reads much of the same ground, so this overstates what it adds. The cost of each measurement is a provisional figure in field.yaml with no recorded source, and the likelihood ratios are provisional too.

content.title: Calibration report
content.subtitle: The survey's forecasts against what was drilled
summary: 45 survey points predicted in 3 projects, 38 of them drilled; 34 of the drilled points had their prediction recorded before drilling.
Only the 34 predictions recorded before drilling are scored: a prediction recorded after its borehole was drilled may have been made knowing what the borehole found.
Depth to basement: 17 of 23 found basement inside the P10 to P90 band (74 percent), where a calibrated band would hold between 15 and 21. The band reads as calibrated.
Chance of success: a Brier score of 0.214 over 28 forecasts, against 0.267 for the prior alone (lower is better).
Hit rates are given by geology unit, survey team and contractor wherever a group has at least 5 boreholes whose outcome is known.

sections.heading: Depth to basement
paragraphs: Where the range of models was sampled, the survey gives the depth to basement a band: the 10th to the 90th percentile (P10 to P90) of the models that fit. A calibrated band holds the depth found four times in five, so about 80 percent of the boreholes should find basement inside it, about 10 percent above it and about 10 percent below it.

Of the 34 boreholes drilled at forecast points, 17 found basement inside the band, 3 above it and 3 below it. 11 stopped short of basement where the band allows it to lie deeper still, and 0 had no band to compare with; neither of these can be judged.
17 of the 23 judged, 74 percent, found basement inside the band. A calibrated band would hold between 15 and 21 of 23 at least nine times in ten.
That is as many as a calibrated band would hold.
Where basement was found, it lay on average 2.48 m shallower than the best-fitting model put it, and 3.4 m from it either way, over 20 boreholes.

sections.heading: The chance of success
paragraphs: Each forecast gave the chance that a borehole at its point would succeed, as the odds define success: a tested yield of at least 1 m3/h. A forecast is scored where its borehole's outcome is known, from a pumping test or from the status the driller recorded.
5 drilled forecast points had no chance worked out, and 1 has no known outcome yet; neither is scored.
Of the 28 outcomes scored, 11 rest on a pumping test, 11 on a failure the driller recorded and 6 on the driller's word of success without a test.
The forecasts gave on average 49 percent, and 10 of the 28 boreholes succeeded, 36 percent.
The Brier score is 0.214: the mean of the squared difference between each forecast chance and its outcome, 1 or 0 (Brier, 1950). Zero is perfect, and an even chance forecast every time scores 0.250.
The prior alone, the chance before any survey, would have scored 0.267, so the survey's evidence improved on it by 20 percent.

The reliability diagram sets the share that succeeded in each band of forecast chance beside the band's mean forecast (Murphy and Winkler, 1977). Calibrated forecasts lie on the diagonal; a band holding few forecasts says little.

sections.heading: Hit rates
paragraphs: A hit rate is the share of boreholes that succeeded, of those whose outcome is known. It is given for each geology unit, survey team and contractor with at least 5 such boreholes, and below that the table says there are too few to judge. Every drilled point counts here, whenever its prediction was recorded. The last column is the mean chance forecast before drilling, over the boreholes with a known outcome, to set beside the rate.

sections.heading: What this report does not say
bullets: It pools only the project files it was given; a borehole whose file is not among them is not counted.
4 drilled points were predicted after drilling. They are left out of the band and the odds, though counted in the hit rates.
Without a pumping test, success is the status the driller recorded, and a borehole recorded as successful may not reach the yield the odds count as success.
Names are grouped as they were written, so two spellings of one team or contractor make two groups.
The minimum numbers of boreholes, 10 for the band and the odds and 5 for a hit rate, are provisional.
It changes nothing the toolkit predicts: the priors and the bands stay as they are until a named person adopts a new calibration.

references: Brier, G. W. (1950). Verification of forecasts expressed in terms of probability. Monthly Weather Review, 78(1), 1-3.

Murphy, A. H. and Winkler, R. L. (1977). Reliability of subjective probability forecasts of precipitation and temperature. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C (Applied Statistics), 26(1), 41-47.

Success means a yield of at least 3.6 m3/h (1.00 L/s) at the dry-season water level, the handpump design rate in the configuration.

The prior is 10 percent (between 1 and 23), for the BGS class I-L on the USGS unit Pi: BGS Low productivity, 0.1 to 0.5 L/s (O Dochartaigh 2021, Tables 3 and 4). No cited source separates the Freetown Complex unit within the class, so the class's yields apply. Read as the quartiles of a lognormal spread, 0.1 and 0.5 L/s put 10 percent of boreholes at or above 1.00 L/s. It is held as firmly as 10 boreholes would hold it, and has not been calibrated against boreholes drilled here.
The range of models has not been sampled at , so the depth to basement and whether it was resolved are left out (a factor of 1 each); sample the range to use them.

Basis: the prior from success_prior.csv and the likelihood ratios from success_evidence.yaml; calibration: calibration set 3, fitted on 2027-03-01 to 12 boreholes and adopted by A. Kamara on 2027-03-02. The band is the 10th to 90th percentile of a Beta prior with the table's effective sample size, carried through the same factors; the factors themselves are provisional choices. The suitability score is kept beside these odds for comparison. Calibration set 3 reads the USGS unit pCm with clay up to 31.5 ohm-m and fresh basement from 1,500 ohm-m.

facies.ca_hco3: The water is a Ca-HCO3 type (Ca 65%, Mg 22%, Na+K 13%; HCO3 76%, Cl 15%, SO4 9%, in milliequivalent percent): a fresh, recently recharged water of the kind weathering of silicate rock gives; typical of shallow basement groundwater.
facies.na_hco3: The water is a Na+K-HCO3 type (Ca 13%, Mg 7%, Na+K 80%; HCO3 75%, Cl 15%, SO4 10%, in milliequivalent percent): a bicarbonate water in which sodium and potassium have replaced calcium, which points to longer contact with the rock or to ion exchange in a clayey weathered zone.
facies.mixed_hco3: The water is a mixed-cation-HCO3 type (Ca 40%, Mg 25%, Na+K 35%; HCO3 63%, Cl 30%, SO4 7%, in milliequivalent percent): a bicarbonate water with no single dominant cation, in which calcium and magnesium together still outweigh sodium and potassium; a fresh water of the kind weathering of silicate rock gives, with the sodium share pointing to feldspar weathering or some ion exchange along the flow path.
facies.na_cl: The water is a Na+K-Cl type (Ca 10%, Mg 10%, Na+K 80%; HCO3 14%, Cl 80%, SO4 6%, in milliequivalent percent): a sodium chloride water, which in this setting points to salinity from the coast, an estuary or evaporation rather than to rock weathering.
facies.ca_cl: The water is a Ca-Cl type (Ca 68%, Mg 11%, Na+K 20%; HCO3 23%, Cl 68%, SO4 9%, in milliequivalent percent): a calcium chloride water, which is unusual in fresh basement groundwater; it can point to saline water exchanging with the aquifer or to pollution, and is worth checking against the sample's provenance.
facies.mixed_cl: The water is a mixed-cation-Cl type (Ca 37%, Mg 29%, Na+K 34%; HCO3 19%, Cl 71%, SO4 10%, in milliequivalent percent): a chloride water with no single dominant cation, which points to salinity or pollution mixed into the groundwater rather than to rock weathering alone.
facies.so4: The water is a Ca-SO4 type (Ca 50%, Mg 25%, Na+K 25%; HCO3 25%, Cl 12%, SO4 62%, in milliequivalent percent): a sulfate water, which is unusual in basement ground and worth checking against the sample's provenance.
facies.ca_mixed_anion: The water is a Ca-mixed-anion type (Ca 75%, Mg 12%, Na+K 12%; HCO3 38%, Cl 32%, SO4 30%, in milliequivalent percent): a water with no single dominant anion, of mixed origin or in transition between types.
facies.mixed: The water is a mixed-cation-mixed-anion type (Ca 38%, Mg 30%, Na+K 33%; HCO3 38%, Cl 32%, SO4 30%, in milliequivalent percent): a mixed water with no single dominant ion pair.

requirements: No input is a bundled example file.
Logged to 70 m with 14 lithological intervals.
Every reading carried a unit the toolkit could read.
1 step with discharge, static water level 9.44 m.

The safe yield of 0.39 m3/h (0.22 to 0.71) is indicative, not established: the test pumped for 30 minutes, below the 240 needed to see late-time behaviour, so the yield is extrapolated 4.2 log cycles of time; the whole test lies inside the 117-minute casing-storage period, so its drawdown is the borehole emptying rather than the aquifer responding; no transmissivity method fitted to standard and the Cooper-Jacob value is adopted as the best available.
The health panel was run and every result was evaluable.
Each decision number carries a band: Safe yield and Pump intake below the top of the casing.
No module reported a fatal problem with the data.

Every reading carried a unit the toolkit could read.
1 step with discharge, static water level 9.44 m.

The safe yield of 0.39 m3/h (0.22 to 0.71) is indicative, not established: the test pumped for 30 minutes, below the 240 needed to see late-time behaviour, so the yield is extrapolated 4.2 log cycles of time; the whole test lies inside the 117-minute casing-storage period, so its drawdown is the borehole emptying rather than the aquifer responding; no transmissivity method fitted to standard and the Cooper-Jacob value is adopted as the best available.
Each decision number carries a band: Safe yield and Pump intake below the top of the casing.
No module reported a fatal problem with the data.

full: Drilling of the borehole to 70 m by Air rotary (DTH hammer).

Construction designed with 5 inch uPVC casing, 19 m of screen, no gravel pack (the 19 mm annulus is too thin to place one) and sanitary seal to 20 m; the drilling log records no casing string as installed.
Development of the borehole by air lifting until clear.
Water quality sampling and laboratory analysis.

confidence_reasons: each step ran for 50 minutes, below the 60 needed to see late-time behaviour, so the yield is extrapolated 4.0 log cycles of time
each step lies inside the 80-minute casing-storage period, so its drawdown is the borehole emptying rather than the aquifer responding
no transmissivity method fitted to standard and the Cooper-Jacob value is adopted as the best available
short_steps.pump_depth_basis: Pump intake at 47 m: the static level 10.0 m plus the 2 m dry-season reserve, the 31.5 m of drawdown the long-term yield is projected to use and 3 m of submergence; the test itself drew the level to 34.5 m at 3 m3/h. The safety factor is kept on the rate, not spent on raising the pump.
short_steps.envelope_basis: Range over transmissivity 1.7-3.7 m2/day, storativity 0.0001-0.01, effective radius 0.075-0.15 m and a dry-season decline of 1-4 m. Design to the lower figure where the supply must not fail in a dry year.
flags: Each step ran for 50 minutes, below the 60 minutes needed to see late-time behaviour; the yield is extrapolated 4.0 log cycles of time to the 365-day design period and should be treated as indicative.

With a 5 inch casing and a specific capacity of 0.13 m3/h per m, casing storage controls the drawdown for the first 80 minutes (Schafer's rule); each step pumped for 50 minutes, entirely inside it. The Cooper-Jacob and Theis fits see the borehole emptying rather than the aquifer. No fit outside that period can be adopted, so the Cooper-Jacob value is adopted only as the best available and the Theis value is reported but not adopted.

No method fitted to standard (Cooper-Jacob 2.50 m2/day, its fitted window 5-50 minutes lies inside the 80-minute casing-storage period; Theis curve fit 2.50 m2/day, each 50-minute step lies inside the 80-minute casing-storage period). The Cooper-Jacob value of 2.50 m2/day is adopted as the best available, so the yield rests on a fit that does not meet it.

positions.note: The site is at T, Western Area, 8.37587 N, 13.10237 W.
positions.geology: The site lies on the unit the USGS Geologic Map of Africa maps as Holocene (Qe). Bullom Group (Q, Tb), Miocene to Recent. Sands, clays, clayey sands and lignite over the coastal lowland; alluvium along the drainage. Intergranular, generally the best yields available without deep drilling. Shallow water tables mean the protective cover is thin, so siting must keep clear of latrines and surface drainage. The BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas classes the aquifer here as Unconsolidated intergranular aquifer - moderate to high productivity (tertiary-quaternary unconsolidated sediments). Groundwater potential depends on the thickness of the weathered zone and the degree of fracturing beneath it, which the soundings below resolve.

positions.note: The site is at T, Port Loko district, 8.40000 N, 13.18000 W.
positions.geology: The site lies on the unit the USGS Geologic Map of Africa maps as Paleozoic Igneous (Pi). Freetown Layered Complex (Jf), Jurassic (about 193 Ma). Layered gabbro, norite and anorthosite; a basic to ultrabasic intrusion forming the Freetown peninsula hills. Massive and crystalline, with negligible primary porosity. Groundwater is confined to the weathered mantle and to fracture and joint sets; yields are modest and highly site-dependent, so the fracture target is the whole of the siting problem. The BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas classes the aquifer here as Igneous intrusive aquifer - low productivity (igneous intrusive). Groundwater potential depends on the thickness of the weathered zone and the degree of fracturing beneath it, which the soundings below resolve.

positions.note: The site is at T, Kono district, 9.39200 N, 10.39600 W.
positions.geology: The site lies on the unit the USGS Geologic Map of Africa maps as Mesozoic Igneous (Mi). Dolerite (Jd), Jurassic. Dolerite, intruded as dykes and sheets cutting the basement. A dyke is usually a barrier rather than an aquifer, but its margins are commonly fractured and its contact with the country rock can concentrate flow. The dyke itself is the wrong target; the contact beside it may be the right one. Groundwater potential depends on the thickness of the weathered zone and the degree of fracturing beneath it, which the soundings below resolve.

positions.note: The site is at T, Karene district, 9.49670 N, 12.24050 W.
positions.geology: The site lies on the unit the USGS Geologic Map of Africa maps as Precambrian (pCm). Precambrian basement, chiefly Leonean granite (LG, Lg, PLg, LM, Er, Lkm, Lkt), Archaean to Palaeoproterozoic. Crystalline basement, but not one rock. Cross-tabbed against the bundled BGS hydrogeology on a 1.4 km national grid, 87% of this class is basement aquifer and 12% is consolidated sedimentary with fracture flow - the Rokel River Group belt through Port Loko, Kambia, Moyamba and Tonkolili. On the 2017 map the basement part is chiefly Leonean granite (LG), with Liberian granite (Lg), migmatitic gneiss (PLg, LM), the Magbele and Tapr formations (Lkm, Lkt) and a mylonite zone. Mostly the crystalline basement aquifer this toolkit is built for: no primary porosity, water in the weathered and fractured zone above fresh rock, yield following regolith thickness and the fracture set at the weathered-fresh contact. But this class is not one rock, and where it covers the Rokel River metasediments the aquifer is fracture flow in indurated beds with shales acting as aquicludes - a different target. Read the aquifer map beside it: the BGS layer separates the two where this one does not. The BGS Africa Groundwater Atlas classes the aquifer here as Basement aquifer - low productivity (precambrian craton). Groundwater potential depends on the thickness of the weathered zone and the degree of fracturing beneath it, which the soundings below resolve.

unplaced_geology.geology: The project area lies within the Freetown Basic Complex. The Freetown Complex is a layered gabbroic anorthosite intrusion emplaced against gneisses and schists of the Kasila Group, and it forms part of the Peninsula and Banana Islands. It is thought to have been formed by multiple injections of magma that occurred intermittently. Groundwater potential within the Freetown Basic Complex is found within weathered and fractured zones of these igneous (crystalline) rocks. Groundwater quality and quantity can be high if the borehole is properly located through appropriate hydrogeological and geophysical investigations.

The project area lies within the crystalline basement terrain of Sierra Leone, where groundwater occurs mainly within the weathered overburden (regolith) and in fractured zones of the underlying bedrock. The weathered zone develops on granites, gneisses and related rocks, and its thickness and degree of fracturing control the groundwater potential. Groundwater quality and quantity can be favourable where the borehole position is properly located through appropriate hydrogeological and geophysical investigations.

sheets.title: Pumping test field sheet: borehole KTL-01
sheets.code: Sheet code GWT-FK/1|pumping|Rokel 2026|KTL-01. Scan it, or type it in, to match this sheet to its project and borehole.
notes: Casing storage: if the transmissivity is as low as 1 m2/day, the water levels of the first 307 minutes may show the 5 inch casing, with its 1.25 inch riser, emptying rather than the aquifer (31 minutes at 10 m2/day).
Constant discharge test: do not stop the pump before 307 minutes, the longer of that time and the shortest constant test the analysis accepts, 240 minutes.
Step test: run every step for at least 60 minutes, and the first for at least 307 minutes, since the drawdown is fitted on the first step.
A shorter test is safe only once the measured drawdown shows a shorter casing-storage time. The pumping test co-pilot or the office works that out from the discharge and the drawdown.
Read the water level at each minute in the Time column, counted from the moment the pump starts. After 120 minutes, read every 30 minutes.
When the pump stops, start the clock again from zero and read the recovery at the same minutes.
sheets.discharge_note: Record the discharge of every step. Time a bucket of known volume three times; the rate in m3/h is 3.6 times the litres divided by the mean seconds. A step with no discharge is written as Not measured, with the reason.
sheets.transcribe: The tables below have the columns of the standard pumping test workbook, so a filled sheet is typed into it cell for cell.

cards.title: Quick card: pumping test reading schedule
lines: Read the water level at these minutes after the pump starts, then every 30 minutes.
When the pump stops, start the clock again from zero and read the recovery at the same minutes.

tables.caption: Reading minutes

notes: Casing storage: if the transmissivity is as low as 1 m2/day, the water levels of the first 307 minutes may show the 5 inch casing, with its 1.25 inch riser, emptying rather than the aquifer (31 minutes at 10 m2/day).
Constant discharge test: do not stop the pump before 307 minutes, the longer of that time and the shortest constant test the analysis accepts, 240 minutes.

A shorter test is safe only once the measured drawdown shows a shorter casing-storage time. The pumping test co-pilot or the office works that out from the discharge and the drawdown.

cards.title: Quick card: VES Schlumberger spacings
lines: A sounding reaches a depth of about 0.5 times its largest AB/2. Peg down the table until the depth reached is at least the target depth, and stop there.
AB is always at least 5 times MN, and MN is widened before AB passes 20 times it. Where MN changes, read the same AB/2 again with the new MN, and keep both readings.

tables.caption: Schlumberger spacings

cards.title: Quick card: disinfecting the borehole with chlorine
lines: Shock dose of 20 mg of chlorine per litre: add 1 litre of 0.2 percent chlorine solution for every 100 litres of water standing in the well, and do not pump for at least 4 hours.
A 0.2 percent solution holds 2 g of chlorine per litre: dissolve about 3.1 g of 65 percent HTH powder in each litre of water.
Water in the well, in litres, is 0.785 times the square of the casing inner diameter in mm, times the water column in m, divided by 1,000.

tables.caption: Litres of 0.2 percent solution (L) and grams of 65 percent HTH (g), by water column and casing inner diameter.

notes: Basis: the toolkit's supervision checklist (borehole disinfected with chlorine at 20 mg per litre, after Adekile, 2014) and its dose calculator, which follows WHO. Where the programme's own disinfection procedure sets a different dose, it takes precedence.

references: Adekile, D. (2014). Supervising Water Well Drilling: a Guide for Supervisors. RWSN/Skat, St Gallen.
World Health Organization (2022). Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality, 4th edition incorporating the first and second addenda. Geneva: World Health Organization.

summary: Drawn up on 2024-06-01. Of the 4 boreholes in the register, 4 have a visit due, on 1 round.
words.method: Each mechanic's round starts at the stop that has been due the longest (a visit with nothing to count from is taken as due on the day the round is drawn up) and goes each time to the nearest stop not yet visited, measured in a straight line on the ellipsoid to the metre, a tie going to the lower identifier. This puts the stops in an order; it is not an optimal route, and it knows nothing of roads, rivers or the rains.
words.intervals: A sanitary inspection is due every 6 months and a water quality sample every 12, counted from the last one recorded or, where there is none, from commissioning; a routine inspection of the pump and rising main at the interval the borehole's design sets for its rising main, or every 6 months where the record carries none. A visit is overdue 30 days after it falls due, and a borehole with no record to count from is due now. These intervals are the programme's settings, choices made here and not a standard.

words.method: Each mechanic's round starts at the stop that has been due the longest (a visit with nothing to count from is taken as due on the day the round is drawn up) and goes each time to the nearest stop not yet visited, measured in a straight line on the ellipsoid to the metre, a tie going to the lower identifier. words.intervals: A sanitary inspection is due every 6 months and a water quality sample every 12, counted from the last one recorded or, where there is none, from commissioning; a routine inspection of the pump and rising main at the interval the borehole's design sets for its rising main, or every 6 months where the record carries none. A visit is overdue 30 days after it falls due, and a borehole with no record to count from is due now. These intervals are the programme's settings, choices made here and not a standard.

summary: Drawn up on 2024-06-01. Of the 2 boreholes in the register, 2 have a visit due, on 1 round.
words.method: Each mechanic's round starts at the stop that has been due the longest (a visit with nothing to count from is taken as due on the day the round is drawn up) and goes each time to the nearest stop not yet visited, measured in a straight line on the ellipsoid to the metre, a tie going to the lower identifier. This puts the stops in an order; it is not an optimal route, and it knows nothing of roads, rivers or the rains.
words.intervals: A sanitary inspection is due every 6 months and a water quality sample every 12, counted from the last one recorded or, where there is none, from commissioning; a routine inspection of the pump and rising main at the interval the borehole's design sets for its rising main, or every 6 months where the record carries none. A visit is overdue 30 days after it falls due, and a borehole with no record to count from is due now. These intervals are the programme's settings, choices made here and not a standard.
